method.unit: partial case assignment per canonical entity or scenario
method.boundary: structured fields only; prose is not classified by this lift
method.limitation: This is a lower bound on corpus coverage. Unknown coordinates mean not machine-authored yet, not impossible.

declarations.basis: The scenario starts after a submitted application and names the ATS application process.
The defining observation is silence after submission; a later generic disposition does not identify the cause.
The compatible mechanisms include stale, expired, parser-failed, quota-driven, and speculative-pool explanations.
No scenario field or linked observation states whether the job was onsite, hybrid, or remote.
The scenario does not reveal whether anyone inside or outside the employer can reopen or alter the condition.
The scenario records submitted material but no candidate-side constraint or exchange condition.
The diagnostic preset stage is screening, and the title names an automated knockout.
The scenario includes a generic closer-alignment rejection template as its first observation.
The template says closer alignment while the scenario frame treats it as a filter result.
Rigid uncontextualized filters are rule-shaped blocks, not stochastic noise or a named incentive.
The observations combine outreach and rejection; the scenario does not say whether the candidate applied inbound.
The scenario does not mention workplace format, city anchoring, or in-office cadence.
The scenario describes rigid filters but not whether the employer has override slack inside the process.

source.title: Vendor process blocked by client-site terms

declarations.basis: The vendor presents the candidate, but the client owns the external approval and site conditions.
The candidate reaches the client through a vendor or agency process rather than direct employer intake.
The client-account funnel places labour through a vendor contract and billable client demand.
The defining feature is an end client deciding profile approval and working terms.
The seat exists because client demand funds vendor work, even if the candidate never sees the commercial contract.
This scenario is the signed-contract branch, not a speculative tender or unwon bid.
The economics run through a client billing rate and vendor margin rather than only internal payroll.
The blocking condition is work at a client site, not merely a timezone overlap or remote payroll list.
The place of work is anchored to the client facility or client-controlled delivery site.
The scenario represents a regular client-site presence requirement rather than occasional visits.
The vendor and client jointly shape the outcome; the direct employer panel is not the sole decider.
The condition belongs to the client gate outside the vendor's immediate recruiting process.
The client-site rule either permits the candidate's working arrangement or blocks placement.
The gate is a site condition imposed on the seat, not comparison within a finalist cohort.
The client site term functions as a delivery rule rather than an interviewer's preference.
Any waiver or alternative site must be granted by the client, not by the vendor recruiter.
The scenario is defined by the candidate being unable to satisfy the client-site attendance term.
The client's site requirement and the candidate's available work arrangement do not overlap in this case.
The candidate usually sees a fit or alignment message while the client-site ownership remains opaque.
The visible terminal artifact is a vendor or client rejection rather than a contract execution.
Client-site conditions commonly turn care, access, and border constraints into gates without proving discriminatory intent.
The client gate and commercial site terms are usually not visible in the original vendor contact.

source.title: Rejected, then the same role is posted again

declarations.basis: The scenario begins from a candidate process that reaches rejection before a public repost is observed.
The title and observations require closure followed by a materially similar repost.
The terminal signal is the role being closed or reposted rather than a final cause attribution.
Internal-fill is compatible, but the scenario explicitly excludes proving that someone was already chosen.
Budget cancellation and role redefinition are both compatible, so funding cannot be read from the surface.
The repost comparison says the requirement body is similar, not what worksite format it contains.
The candidate can preserve finalist standing, but no concrete candidate-side condition is authored here.
The diagnostic preset stage is post-offer and includes accepted-offer delay or revocation.
The terminal observation is delayed start date or post-signing revocation after acceptance.
The scenario summary names start-date slippage as the epilogue-shaped event.
The observation names jurisdiction or work-eligibility grounds without specifying a single country.
Down-levelling and delayed starts can occur in permanent, contract, or contract-to-hire arrangements.
Jurisdiction or eligibility is not the same as where the work must be performed.
The scenario does not state whether the employer can move level, start date, or compensation internally.
The scenario names candidate-facing changes but not what concessions the candidate can trade against them.
The diagnostic preset stage is sourcing and the scenario is about posting refresh behavior.
The scenario explicitly combines active applicants with silence after submission.
The scenario names a ghost requisition and an identical refreshed posting body.
The distinctive public signal is a refreshed or reposted vacancy, not a final causal explanation.
A refreshed posting may be funded, stale, speculative, or awaiting approval.
The scenario does not say whether the refreshed posting is onsite, hybrid, or remote.
The candidate can see the refreshed posting and silence but cannot see the requisition owner or funding state.
The candidate and recruiter encounter the requirement, while employer policy defines what cadence is disqualifying.
The candidate entered through a posted process and reached an initial screen.
The scenario describes a job process rather than a temporary shift assignment or freelance statement of work.
No client, public-sector, or regulated-profession overlay is part of this scenario.
The scenario is specifically about a named weekly office cadence rather than optional occasional attendance.
A fixed hybrid cadence must be attached to a concrete city or office location to become a real constraint.
The authored case represents the common two-to-three-day hybrid requirement rather than occasional attendance.
The attendance rule is an employer-side policy or team operating constraint, not an external legal bar.
Once the weekly cadence is fixed, the candidate either can meet it for this office or cannot.
The failure is against an attendance condition, not against another candidate's score.
The condition is a format rule about where work must happen, not a subjective panel judgement.
The employer may be able to move the cadence or city rule internally, but that exception is not in the recruiter screen itself.
The candidate could trade format for another condition, such as relocation timing or fewer office days, rather than simply accept or refuse.
Both sides may have some latitude, but the scenario does not show an actual negotiated overlap.
A generic remote-or-hybrid label hides the weekly burden until after the candidate has already spent screening effort.
The under-specified worksite condition comes from how the role is described, not from an ATS parsing failure.
The observed terminal artifact is a rejection after compatibility screening, not a successful hire or offer change.
Fixed attendance cadence can be the operative gate for caregiving, access, and displacement constraints without proving bias.
The candidate sees the late attendance condition but not whether an internal exception route exists.
The diagnostic preset stage is technical and the title places the case after a panel.
The scenario includes a rejection that names an internal hire as the outcome.
The internal-hire outcome makes an internal cohort relevant, while not proving bad faith or timing.
The candidate sees rescheduling, silence, and an internal-hire statement but not the freeze decision.
The freeze could be budget, approval, prioritization, or internal-fill driven.
The scenario concerns interview-panel timing and does not state where the job is performed.
The scenario does not reveal who could unblock the freeze or internal-fill decision.
The observation is a recruiter message, but the contractability list belongs to employer policy rather than the individual recruiter.
The scenario starts from a posted remote role and a candidate entering the ordinary hiring funnel.
The mechanism concerns issuing an employment contract, not a freelance statement of work.
The role is held in the atlas' default software hiring domain unless a client or regulated sector is named.
The work is described as remote, but the accepted place is bounded by a national contractability list.
The operative worksite constraint is not a desk or commute radius; it is the country where an entity or provider can issue the contract.
The case has no regular office attendance; the failure is legal/payroll coverage, not a required office week.
The mismatch exists because residence and contractability coverage do not sit inside the same local hiring regime.
The constraint is maintained by employer policy and payroll coverage, even if the recruiter only relays it.
A country either appears on the employer's contractability list for this role or it does not.
The candidate is blocked by a rule about their location, not by comparison with another candidate.
The mechanism is a compliance and payroll rule rather than an interviewer judgement.
For this process the recruiter cannot add a legal entity or payroll provider to cover the candidate's country.
The scenario does not state whether relocation, a different contract form, or withdrawal was possible for the candidate.
Employer latitude is fixed, but candidate latitude is not stated, so overlap cannot be computed from the authored case.
The closing message names the jurisdiction or work-eligibility ground rather than burying it in a generic template.
The process closes without a hire; the specific ground is legible, but the artifact remains a rejection.
The candidate sees the stated location ground, but not the internal payroll coverage route or exception calendar.

source.title: Remote role bounded by timezone overlap

declarations.basis: The recruiter can ask the timezone question, but the team and employer policy define the overlap requirement.
The scenario begins with a candidate pursuing a remote role through the ordinary process.
No contractor, vendor, seasonal, or freelance arrangement is part of this scenario.
The scenario uses remote team coordination in a software role as the default atlas domain.
The work can be performed away from an office, but the team still imposes a time-zone overlap rule.
The operative anchor is not a city or country; it is the hours a candidate can overlap with the team.
The remote role may still require occasional synchronous overlap, but not a regular office week.
The overlap requirement is owned by the team or employer policy, not by an outside client or statute.
A required overlap band either fits the candidate's working hours or it does not.
The case is blocked by a schedule rule, not by relative ranking against another applicant.
The overlap requirement is a coordination rule rather than a taste judgement.
The team might move rituals or overlap hours internally, but no outside party must approve that change.
The candidate may shift hours only by trading against care, health, or local-time constraints.
The scenario shows potential latitude on both sides, but not an actual agreed overlap window.
The closing reason can truthfully name hours or timezone rather than only general alignment.
The process terminates without an offer, even when the reason names a time constraint.
Overlap windows can turn care schedules, health boundaries, and cross-border time differences into hiring gates.
The candidate sees the overlap ask, but not how movable the team's schedule really is.

source.title: Ukrainian reservation status meets worksite constraint

declarations.basis: The candidate and recruiter encounter the constraint, while employer policy and public policy determine reservation and registration treatment.
The scenario starts from an ordinary hiring process rather than a rehire or referral route.
Reservation and employment-status questions arise around an employment role, not a freelance statement of work.
The scenario keeps the atlas' software hiring baseline and varies the Ukrainian administrative condition.
The case is about a concrete attendance requirement rather than a fully remote global role.
The role is anchored to a Ukrainian hiring location rather than only to payroll entity coverage.
A minimal regular attendance requirement is enough to interact with registration and movement constraints.
The scenario is explicitly about Ukrainian military registration and employer reservation status.
The structural case concerns a role whose feasibility depends on employer-linked reservation treatment.
Military registration interacts with gendered service rules and age bands even when the scenario does not assert discriminatory motive.
The decisive condition comes from an administrative regime outside the ordinary interview evaluation.
Reservation status is not owned solely by the recruiter or hiring manager inside the interview loop.
For a particular role and candidate, the administrative status either satisfies the condition or it does not.
The block concerns whether this candidate can occupy this role under the condition, not relative merit against another candidate.
The coordinate is a public-policy and employer-policy rule, not a panel taste judgement.
If an exception or reservation route exists, it is controlled outside the individual recruiter conversation.
The candidate cannot personally change the employer's reservation capacity during the hiring loop.
The authored case is one where the required worksite and administrative status do not produce an available agreement.
The closing condition can be named as eligibility or administrative status rather than disguised as general fit.
The scenario uses the post-offer delay or revocation observation as the visible terminal signal.
The case reaches a post-acceptance administrative block rather than stopping at screening.
The candidate can see the administrative issue but not the whole route by which an employer-side reservation decision is made.
